article.title: [abc.net.au] Lancet researchers urge health emergency declaration as climate losses mount
article.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

Drought acceleration: The area affected by extreme drought expanded more than 700% faster in the decade after the Paris Agreement took effect than in the previous decade (abc.com.py). Health preparedness: Only 56 of the World Health Organization’s 194 member states had adapted health systems to climate risks, while 75 countries had early-warning systems for extreme weather (abc.com.py, straitstimes.com). Research funding gap: Climate-related medical research funding reached $316 million in 2024 after rising sevenfold, but 84% went to researchers in wealthy countries (straitstimes.com, insideclimatenews.org).
article._kite_context:
Perspective: Jeni Miller, executive director of the Global Climate and Health Alliance, said healthcare resilience cannot compensate for unchecked warming and argued that cutting the drivers of climate change is essential to protecting health (insideclimatenews.org). (Inside Climate News)
Perspective: Diana Picon Manyari, international climate senior director at Health Care Without Harm, called for health professionals to have a seat at COP31 and said climate-health financing commitments remain difficult to access (insideclimatenews.org). (Inside Climate News)
Perspective: Professor Paul Beggs, a Macquarie University climate-health expert, said Australia’s role as COP president should bring progress on emissions cuts and pointed to deaths from heatwaves and bushfire smoke in Australia as evidence that no region is immune (ABC News Australia)
Quote: "The rate of increase in many climate-related health threats is accelerating, while heat deaths linked to climate change have reached a record-high, and the economic toll is battering vulnerable sectors and communities the hardest." (Marina Romanello, executive director of the Lancet Countdown, ScienceAlert)

Timeline: 9 November 2026: COP31 is scheduled to open in Antalya, Türkiye (lemonde.fr).

article.title: [scitechdaily.com] Researchers identify new dinosaur genus from fossil found in England in 2001
article.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Paleontologists have classified a fossil found in a Surrey clay quarry in 2001 as Paludohadros proudlovii, a previously unknown genus and species of plant-eating dinosaur that lived about 125 million years ago. The four-legged animal was about 5 metres long and weighed an estimated 1.5 to 2 metric tons, but its bones indicate it had not reached adulthood. The fossil was donated to London’s Natural History Museum, where it remained for years before a detailed comparison with other iguanodontians revealed distinguishing features. The identification also helped researchers identify fossils collected from the same quarry in the 1950s as belonging to the newly named dinosaur. article.title: [ScienceDaily] Earth's ice ages may have been driven by a hidden ocean chain reaction
article.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Scientists have uncovered a surprising connection between Earth's opposite poles that may help explain how the planet plunged into past ice ages. New research suggests that as massive ice sheets expanded across the Northern Hemisphere, they cooled Atlantic Ocean waters that eventually traveled south toward Antarctica. This cooling may have disrupted Southern Ocean circulation, allowing the ocean to absorb and store more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, further cooling the planet.

article.title: [sci.news] Cambridge study finds comets rarely delivered life’s ingredients to Earth
article.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A University of Cambridge-led study finds it was extremely unlikely that comets delivered enough hydrogen cyanide, a chemical used in proposed pathways to life, to early Earth. The study, published in Scientific Reports on Oct. 28, used computer simulations to model comet evolution, atmospheric entry and impacts. The team says most impacts would destroy the molecule or fail to leave it at a useful concentration. Of the researchers’ 100,000 simulated histories, 54% included no comet impact that delivered hydrogen cyanide at concentrations considered sufficient for prebiotic chemistry. Comet delivery was more likely on Mars, where lower gravity and a thinner atmosphere make successful impacts more feasible, but the study does not establish that it happened there. The authors point to asteroid impacts or chemical processes on Earth as alternatives; outside researchers say the findings test a specific delivery pathway, not every possible comet contribution.

The study, published in Scientific Reports on Oct. 28, used computer simulations to model comet evolution, atmospheric

The authors point to asteroid impacts or chemical processes on Earth as alternatives; outside researchers say the findings test a specific delivery pathway, not every possible comet contribution (sci.news, lavozdegalicia.es, 24horas.cl). Narrow conditions: For hydrogen cyanide to survive and remain useful, the study’s scenarios favor comets larger than 100 meters that move slowly and strike land at an oblique angle (sciencenews.org, reddit.com). Short window: The number of comets striking Earth fell rapidly during the planet’s first 500 million years, leaving only a handful of possible delivery events in the model (phys.org, digitaltrends.com, orf.at). Possible terrestrial settings: Volcanoes and hydrothermal vents are among the proposed sources of organic precursors on Earth (sciencenews.org).
